analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from weighing benefits they can't put a dollar figure on when writing regulations.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one cosponsor, got a single committee hearing in ten months and never came to a vote; the Senate is still in session.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal agencies must weigh a rule's costs against its benefits before issuing it. Some benefits — lives saved, illnesses avoided, cleaner air — are real but hard to translate into dollars. This bill would forbid agencies from considering any benefit they cannot monetize, and would require courts to strike down any final rule that relied on such a factor. It would apply retroactively to rules issued since November 2023, letting companies sue to invalidate existing rules on that ground.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that face federal regulation. By law, a rule whose main benefits cannot be assigned dollar values could not be issued, and companies could sue to invalidate existing rules issued since November 2023 on the ground that they relied on non-monetized benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits agencies from considering any non-monetized or unquantified factor in the regulatory impact or benefit-cost analysis required for proposed and final rules.
Bars the Office of Management and Budget from authorizing or endorsing the use of non-monetized factors, and from considering them in reviewing other agencies' analyses.

Lets any party affected by a rule sue in federal court, and requires a court to declare a final rule invalid if the agency relied on non-monetized factors; the challenge applies to any rule issued on or after November 9, 2023.
Requires agencies to publish the full text, methodology, and rationale of each regulatory impact and benefit-cost analysis alongside the rule.

analysis.who_pays: The public, through weaker or unenforceable protections where the benefits are hard to price — such as clean air and water, workplace safety, public health, and consumer protections. Agencies would be legally unable to justify rules resting on those benefits, and companies could go to court to strike existing ones down.

drawbacks.text: Many significant regulatory benefits — reduced cancer risk, avoided deaths and injuries, ecosystem damage, fraud prevented — resist dollar valuation; the bill would make rules relying on them legally invalid.

The judicial-review provision applies retroactively to rules issued since November 9, 2023, so companies could challenge existing regulations years after they took effect, creating uncertainty for both businesses and the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency requirement — publishing each analysis and its methodology — is a genuine, low-cost gain for the public. But the core prohibition would make it legally impossible for agencies to defend rules whose principal benefits are human health and safety gains that cannot be credibly converted into dollars, and would open existing rules to court challenges. The public would trade visible paperwork for weaker protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in January 2025; ten months later its only action beyond referral was a hearing by the Small Business Committee, and no markup or floor vote has been scheduled while the Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Joni Ernst introduced the bill on January 17, 2025, joined by Sen. James Lankford as its sole cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, where no further action has been taken.
On November 19, 2025, the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship held a hearing on the bill.
No vote has occurred in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet. Because nothing has passed or been blocked, the status quo holds: agencies can still use non-monetized benefits, and existing rules remain in force.

for.name: Sen. Joni Ernst
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; sole cosponsor (1 of 53 Senate Republicans)

for.name: Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on November 19, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Republicans (1 of 53 Senate R cosponsors); the bill never reached a vote, so no opposition positions are on record, and the Homeland Security committee has taken no action since the January 2025 referral.

industries.industry: Heavily regulated industries (energy, manufacturing, chemicals, finance)
industries.note: The bill would bar agencies from counting benefits that cannot be assigned dollar values — such as avoided deaths, illness, or pollution — and let companies sue to invalidate final rules that relied on them, including rules issued since November 2023. Lower compliance costs for these industries come at the expense of the health, safety, and consumer protections those rules provide.

industries.industry: Small businesses and other regulated firms
industries.note: The bill was heard in the Small Business Committee and would reduce the analytical and compliance burden of federal rulemaking for firms of all sizes; small businesses also gain certainty only until a court invalidates an existing rule they had relied on.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor, no markup in its assigned committee after ten months, and only one hearing, the bill is unlikely to reach the Senate floor this Congress; bills at this stage typically die in committee when the session ends.
